learningObjectives: Explain how Rulesets and versioning control rule promotion and locking
Describe the class hierarchy and how rules are organised within classes
Explain how rule inheritance allows child classes to reuse parent rules
Create a new rule by selecting the correct class and Ruleset

elements.description: The basic building block of a Pega application that defines its behavior. Each Rule is an instance of a Rule Type, which determines the type of behavior it models. Pega uses Rules to generate application code in the background.

elements.text: A Rule is an individual instruction; a Ruleset groups related instructions for management. Runtime selection depends on the configured application context, not an automatic download of the latest available version.

elements.description: A template for creating a Rule that models a specific behavior — for example, a Flow Rule models a Process, while other Rule Types model UI, automated Decisions, and more.

elements.term: Automated Rule creation in App Studio
elements.description: As you add Processes, define Steps, and configure Views in the Case Life Cycle, Pega creates and manages the underlying Rules (Flows, Tasks, UI) in the background, letting developers focus on business tasks.

elements.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><title>Rules and Rule Types</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="180" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface-1)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><g font-family="system-ui" font-size="16" fill="var(--pa-ink)"><text x="26" y="42">Rule instance → Rule Type models behavior</text><text x="26" y="76">Modularity benefits: versioning, delegation and reuse</text><text x="26" y="110">Ruleset versions: major-minor-patch, e.g. 01-02-03</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Rule instance → Rule Type models behavior; Modularity benefits: versioning, delegation and reuse; Ruleset versions: major-minor-patch, e.g. 01-02-03. This summarizes the lesson and is not a complete runtime resolution algorithm.

elements.description: Create a new version whenever Case behavior must change. Pega keeps change history — you can review and undo. Each Rule describes specific behavior, so changes are isolated to that Rule only.

Developers delegate a Rule to business users so they can update Case behavior as conditions change while the rest of the application stays unchanged (e.g., Accounting raises an auto-approval threshold from USD 25 to USD 50 without a change request).
Developers reuse Rules whenever an application needs existing behavior, instead of reconfiguring it every time (e.g., reuse one policyholder-info UI form across auto, property, and marine claims).
To increase reusability, use parameters to drive a Rule's logic based on a passed value instead of hard-coded data — reducing code duplication and the time to implement Rule specializations.

elements.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><title>Application Modularity with Rules</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="180" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface-1)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><g font-family="system-ui" font-size="16" fill="var(--pa-ink)"><text x="26" y="42">Reuse existing behavior rather than recreate it</text><text x="26" y="76">Versioning records controlled changes</text><text x="26" y="110">Delegation permits selected business-managed updates</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Reuse existing behavior rather than recreate it; Versioning records controlled changes; Delegation permits selected business-managed updates. This summarizes the lesson and is not a complete runtime resolution algorithm.

elements.description: A group that identifies, stores, and manages the set of Rules defining an application, packaged for distribution. Rulesets can be SHARED between applications to reuse the same Rules (like an album shared across playlists).

An instance of a Ruleset collecting individual Rules. Create a NEW version to update contents (unlocked for edits); best practice is to LOCK older versions. Version format: major-minor-patch (two-digit each), starting at 01-01-01.
The application stack orders Rulesets for lookup. A listed entry covers versions down to the lowest minor and patch in the specified major version, not every earlier major version.

elements.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><title>Rulesets and Versioning</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="180" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface-1)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><g font-family="system-ui" font-size="16" fill="var(--pa-ink)"><text x="26" y="42">01-01-01 → 01-01-02 is a patch increment</text><text x="26" y="76">01-01-01 → 01-02-01 is a minor increment</text><text x="26" y="110">Lock older versions; develop in the appropriate editable context</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: 01-01-01 → 01-01-02 is a patch increment; 01-01-01 → 01-02-01 is a minor increment; Lock older versions; develop in the appropriate editable context. This summarizes the lesson and is not a complete runtime resolution algorithm.

elements.title: Rule Creation & Versioning Decisions

elements.description: In App Studio, Rules are created FOR you as you build the Case Life Cycle, Views, and data. In Dev Studio, you can directly create and manage how a Rule is created and reused to maintain Rule integrity and reusability.
Four fields that uniquely identify a rule: (1) Rule Type (function), (2) Ruleset (grouping), (3) Apply to (target class), (4) Label (display name). These four fields together enable Rule Resolution.
Five paths to the New Record form, each pre-filling context:
items: Create menu: Rule Type, application context and Ruleset
App Explorer: adds the class context
Rule reference: also provides Label/identifier when the reference has a name
Save As: source context, with Identifier, Class or Ruleset changed
Records explorer: application context and Ruleset

elements.description: Copy an existing Rule into a different class or Ruleset to specialize its behavior, preserving the original while creating a variant. At least one of Identifier, Class, or Ruleset must differ from the source.

The source describes a generally four-part instance key: internal Rule Type, applies-to class, identifier and creation timestamp normalized to GMT. Some Rule Types add identifying elements. Do not confuse this key with the entire runtime Rule selection algorithm.

elements.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><title>Rule Creation</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="180" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface-1)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><g font-family="system-ui" font-size="16" fill="var(--pa-ink)"><text x="26" y="42">Select the Rule Type, Applies-To class and Ruleset</text><text x="26" y="76">Use a readable Label; identifier constraints are a separate concern</text><text x="26" y="110">Verify the writable version and intended reuse scope</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Select the Rule Type, Applies-To class and Ruleset; Use a readable Label; identifier constraints are a separate concern; Verify the writable version and intended reuse scope. This summarizes the lesson and is not a complete runtime resolution algorithm.

elements.description: A grouping of Rules by reuse scope. Three class types per application: Work class (Case processing rules), Data class (data model rules), Integration class (connector rules). Classes form the inheritance hierarchy Pega uses to resolve rules at runtime.
A class can contain other classes. A parent class contains another class; a child class is contained by another. A child class can reuse/inherit any Rules defined for its parent class.

Classes are layered most-specific to least-specific. At run time, Pega starts with the most-specific class and expands to more general ones. The class name shows position: TGB-IT-Work is a child of TGB-IT, a child of TGB.

elements.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><title>Classes and Class Hierarchy</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="180" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface-1)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><g font-family="system-ui" font-size="16" fill="var(--pa-ink)"><text x="26" y="42">Classes group Rules by reusable behavior</text><text x="26" y="76">Work, Data and Integration have distinct purposes</text><text x="26" y="110">Search starts with the specific class and expands to ancestors</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Classes group Rules by reusable behavior; Work, Data and Integration have distinct purposes; Search starts with the specific class and expands to ancestors. This summarizes the lesson and is not a complete runtime resolution algorithm.

elements.description: AUTOMATIC inheritance using the existing class-name structure (shared prefix) to determine which Rules are available for reuse. Promotes reuse based on BUSINESS suitability — aggregating Rules at higher levels for departments within that division.

Inheritance where the parent class is EXPLICITLY specified on the class Rule form (not automatic). Lets an application class inherit Rules from OUTSIDE the business class hierarchy (e.g., Work- or Data-). Promotes reuse based on FUNCTIONAL suitability.

Pega searches parent classes via pattern inheritance; if unsuccessful, uses the directed inheritance parent for another pattern search — repeating until reaching @baseclass. If still not found after @baseclass, Pega returns an error.

elements.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 760 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><title>Rule Reuse Through Inheritance</title><rect x="10" y="10" width="740" height="180" rx="12" fill="var(--pa-surface-1)" stroke="var(--pa-brand)"/><g font-family="system-ui" font-size="16" fill="var(--pa-ink)"><text x="26" y="42">Pattern inheritance uses shared class-name prefixes</text><text x="26" y="76">Directed inheritance specifies an explicit parent</text><text x="26" y="110">Work- and Data- reuse can cross the business naming hierarchy</text></g></svg>
elements.caption: Pattern inheritance uses shared class-name prefixes; Directed inheritance specifies an explicit parent; Work- and Data- reuse can cross the business naming hierarchy. This summarizes the lesson and is not a complete runtime resolution algorithm.

examPitfalls.title: Rule vs. Rule Type
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Candidates blur these. A Rule is an INSTANCE of a Rule Type; the Rule Type is the template that determines the behavior modeled.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Remember a Flow Rule (type) models a Process; the specific flow you built is the Rule.

examPitfalls.title: The three modularity benefits
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The Rules and Rule Types topic names versioning, delegation and reuse as the three modularity benefits.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Versioning = history/rollback; Delegation = hand a Rule to business users; Reuse = use existing behavior without rebuilding.

examPitfalls.title: Ruleset version format
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A question asks what format a Ruleset version must follow. Candidates say 'any numbering scheme.' Ruleset versions use a three-segment format (major.minor.patch, e.g., 01-01-01) — all three segments are required.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Read e.g. 01-02-03 as major 01, minor 02, patch 03. New version to edit; lock older versions.

examPitfalls.title: Ruleset naming rules
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Ruleset naming constraints and meaningful Rule Labels are different. Class names use hyphens, so do not claim their constraints are identical to Ruleset names.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Use meaningful names; no Pega prefix; no spaces; ≤32 chars; avoid - _ + and quotes.

examPitfalls.title: The three class types
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Work, Integration, and Data classes get confused. Work = process Cases; Integration = talk to other systems; Data = describe data types.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: If it's about processing a Case → Work; connecting externally → Integration; defining a data type → Data.

examPitfalls.title: Class hierarchy search direction
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A question asks in which direction Pega searches the class hierarchy when resolving a rule. Candidates say 'top-down from the root.' Pega searches UPWARD from the most specific class toward @baseclass — higher specificity is checked first.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Pega starts at the most-specific class and walks UP to more general classes.

examPitfalls.title: Pattern vs. Directed inheritance
examPitfalls.trapDescription: The classic trap: pattern is AUTOMATIC (by class-name prefix, business suitability); directed is EXPLICIT on the class form (functional suitability) and is what lets you inherit standard Pega classes like Work-/Data-.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Automatic + prefix = pattern; explicitly specified parent + reaches standard Pega classes = directed.

examPitfalls.title: @baseclass and resolution failure
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Resolution alternates pattern then directed searches up to the ultimate base class, @baseclass; not finding the Rule there returns an error.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Order: pattern → directed (then pattern again) → … → @baseclass → error if still not found.

examPitfalls.title: Save As requires at least one change
examPitfalls.trapDescription: When using Save As on an existing rule, all fields are pre-filled. A common trap: not changing anything. Pega returns an error unless at least one of Identifier, Class, or Ruleset differs from the source.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Save As = copy + specialize. Must change Identifier, Class, or Ruleset — or Pega blocks creation.

examPitfalls.title: Rule creation method and what auto-fills
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions present a creation path (App Explorer vs. Create menu vs. Rule reference) and ask what's pre-filled. Key difference: Create menu fills Type+app+Ruleset; App Explorer also fills Class; Rule reference also fills Label+ID if the reference name is given.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: More context = more auto-fill. Rule reference fills the most; Create menu fills the least.

examPitfalls.title: Who designs the class hierarchy
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions ask who is responsible for designing the class hierarchy. Candidates say 'the business stakeholder.' The class hierarchy is a technical artifact designed by the System Architect — business users define requirements but do not design the class structure.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: The source says the LSA and project leaders typically plan the hierarchy before building; this is not exclusive ownership by one person.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA configures a Process in the App Studio Case Life Cycle. What type of rule is generated in the underlying Pega platform?

options.text: A Flow Rule — the visual process modeled in App Studio is stored as a Flow Rule in the Pega platform
A Ruleset version — each process configured in App Studio creates a new Ruleset version to hold the change
An Access Role — process definitions in App Studio are stored as Access Role rules that control who can execute them
A Data class — each App Studio Process generates a new Data class to hold the process's field definitions

practiceQuiz.hint: Adding a Process in App Studio creates an underlying Flow Rule in Dev Studio.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The source maps an App Studio Process to a Flow Rule.

optionExplanations.A: The source maps an App Studio Process to a Flow Rule.
optionExplanations.B: Creating a Process does not inherently create a new version container.
optionExplanations.C: Access roles do not model the requested Process behavior.
optionExplanations.D: A data-type class is not the generated Process Rule.

practiceQuiz.scenario: The Accounting team wants to raise the auto-approval threshold for expense reports from USD 500 to USD 1,000 without involving IT. Which Pega feature makes this self-service update possible?

options.text: Delegation — a rule is delegated to a business user so they can update it directly without SA involvement
Versioning — creating a new minor version of the decision rule allows Accounting to change the threshold independently
Reuse — marking the decision rule as a relevant record allows Accounting to copy and modify it
Parametrization alone, with no business maintenance interface or delegated access, automatically lets Accounting change the Rule

practiceQuiz.hint: Enabling business users to update rules themselves without SA help is Delegation.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Explicit delegation gives the selected business users the requested maintenance capability.

optionExplanations.A: Explicit delegation gives the selected business users the requested maintenance capability.
optionExplanations.B: Versioning alone does not grant these users the required editing authority.
optionExplanations.C: Assembly relevance does not itself grant delegated editing rights.
optionExplanations.D: Parameters alone do not establish the requested business maintenance interface.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A developer needs to preserve the existing Rule while preparing an experiment in a separate development context. Which statement correctly describes versioning and branching?

options.text: Create the changed Rule in an appropriate new Ruleset version while retaining the older version
Use a development Branch to isolate the proposed change before reviewed integration
Both described approaches can retain the original; configuration and testing determine the appropriate workflow
Saving the rule to a text file before editing provides a manual backup; paste the original back if the experiment fails

practiceQuiz.hint: A version is created, not checked out as a whole; Rule checkout and versioning are different operations.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Both described mechanisms can retain the original under their configured workflows.

optionExplanations.A: This is a valid versioning approach, but selecting it alone omits the supported branching alternative summarized by C.
optionExplanations.B: This is a valid branching approach, but selecting it alone omits the supported versioning alternative summarized by C.
optionExplanations.C: Both described mechanisms can retain the original under their configured workflows.
optionExplanations.D: A text copy is not the requested managed development context.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A new SA is reviewing a Ruleset named Expense:01-02-03 in Dev Studio and needs to understand what each segment of the version number means. How should you correctly interpret this Ruleset version number?

options.text: Major version 01, minor version 02, patch 03 of the Expense Ruleset — the three segments represent increasing levels of change granularity
Version 1,023 of the Expense application — the hyphens separate digit groups in a single continuous version number
Three separate Rulesets named 01, 02, and 03 that are all part of the Expense application
A three-part date stamp (January 2, 2003) embedded in the version number for release tracking purposes

practiceQuiz.hint: Ruleset version = Major-Minor-Patch. Expense:01-02-03 = major 01, minor 02, patch 03.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The three segments identify major, minor and patch versions.

optionExplanations.A: The three segments identify major, minor and patch versions.
optionExplanations.B: The separators do not form one concatenated application version number.
optionExplanations.C: The segments belong to one Ruleset version, not three containers.
optionExplanations.D: The numeric sequence is not a release date.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA is about to create Rulesets for a new Pega insurance implementation and wants the team to follow consistent naming conventions that avoid conflicts with Pega-reserved names. Which TWO of the following are valid Ruleset naming best practices in Pega?

options.text: Use meaningful names and keep them to 32 characters or fewer — names should be descriptive and within Pega's recommended length
Avoid the 'Pega' and 'Pega-' prefix — this prefix is reserved for Pega's own built-in Rulesets and should not be used for custom Rulesets
Use spaces and dashes freely throughout the name — these characters are supported and encouraged for readability
Name every Ruleset after the implementation layer only — using layer names as Ruleset names is the required convention

practiceQuiz.hint: Meaningful + ≤32 chars + avoid 'Pega' prefix = correct naming practices.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Meaningful names and the documented maximum length support identification. These prefixes are reserved for platform Rulesets.

optionExplanations.A: Meaningful names and the documented maximum length support identification.
optionExplanations.B: These prefixes are reserved for platform Rulesets.
optionExplanations.C: The source restricts spaces and these special characters.
optionExplanations.D: A universal layer-only naming requirement is not stated.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A new SA asks: 'I want to add a field to an existing Case Type. Should I create the field in the Case Type's local Data Model, or in a separate shared data object, and why does it matter?' What is the best practice answer?

options.text: Create it in a shared data object if the field concept is reusable across Case Types (e.g., 'Address'), or in the Case Type's local Data Model if it is specific to only this Case Type — the choice affects reusability
Always create fields in the Case Type's local Data Model — shared data objects are only for fields that will be displayed in reports, not for Case Type fields
Always create fields in a shared data object — Pega requires all fields to be in shared objects and the Case Type's local Data Model is read-only
It does not matter — Pega automatically promotes fields from local Data Models to shared objects after 30 days if they are used in more than one Case Type

practiceQuiz.hint: Local Data Model vs shared data object — what determines the right choice?
practiceQuiz.rationale: Choose the reuse scope appropriate to the actual field concept.

optionExplanations.A: Choose the reuse scope appropriate to the actual field concept.
optionExplanations.B: Local-only duplication is not required for reusable data concepts.
optionExplanations.C: The Case data model is not universally read-only.
optionExplanations.D: The source does not establish automatic promotion after a time interval.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An application needs rules that connect it to an external customer database — connectors, request/response mappings, and integration services. Which class type holds these rules?

options.text: Integration class — stores rules that connect the application to external systems (connectors, mappings, integration services)
Work class — stores the rules describing how Cases are processed (Processes, Stages, Steps)
Data class — stores the rules describing the data model (properties, field specifications)
Access class — stores security rules that control which users can interact with external systems

practiceQuiz.hint: Rules governing external connectivity and integration belong to the Integration class.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Integration classes group external-interaction behavior.

optionExplanations.A: Integration classes group external-interaction behavior.
optionExplanations.B: Work processing has a different grouping purpose.
optionExplanations.C: Data-type definitions have a different grouping purpose.
optionExplanations.D: This invented fourth application class grouping does not answer the question.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which class type contains the rules that describe how to PROCESS Cases — Processes, Stages, decisions, and user interfaces?

options.text: Work class — the class type that holds all rules related to how Cases are executed and processed
Integration class — the class type for external connectivity rules also hosts workflow and decision rules
Data class — the class type for data model definitions also contains the Processes and UI rules
Rule class — a dedicated 'Rule class' holds all Pega rules; Work, Integration, and Data classes are subsets of it

practiceQuiz.hint: Case processing rules (Processes, Stages, UI, decisions) = Work class.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Work classes group Case processing behavior in this lesson.

optionExplanations.A: Work classes group Case processing behavior in this lesson.
optionExplanations.B: External connectivity is a different grouping purpose.
optionExplanations.C: Data-type definitions are different from the stated Case-processing group.
optionExplanations.D: Rule Type classes and application Applies-To groups are not interchangeable.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A System Architect is reviewing the class hierarchy for a TGB project and sees the class TGB-IT-Work. Which statement about the class hierarchy relationship of TGB-IT-Work is correct?

options.text: TGB-IT-Work is a child of TGB-IT, which is a child of TGB — the hyphens define parent-child relationships in pattern inheritance
TGB-IT-Work is the parent of TGB — deeper nesting means higher in the hierarchy, not lower
The hyphens are decorative and carry no semantic meaning in Pega class naming
TGB-IT-Work and TGB are sibling classes with no hierarchical relationship

practiceQuiz.hint: Hyphens define hierarchy: TGB → TGB-IT → TGB-IT-Work (more specific = deeper child).
practiceQuiz.rationale: The provided naming example follows the shared-prefix hierarchy.

optionExplanations.A: The provided naming example follows the shared-prefix hierarchy.
optionExplanations.B: This reverses the parent and child relationship.
optionExplanations.C: The naming structure is relevant to the described pattern hierarchy.
optionExplanations.D: The specified classes are ancestors in this naming example.

practiceQuiz.scenario: At runtime, in what order does Pega search the class hierarchy for a Rule?

options.text: From the most-specific class, expanding outward toward more-general ancestors until the rule is found or @baseclass is reached
From the most-general class (e.g., @baseclass), narrowing down to the most-specific class where the rule was defined
Randomly across all classes — Pega uses a hash to select the class to search first for performance
From the Integration class first, then the Data class, then the Work class — class type determines search order

practiceQuiz.hint: Rule resolution = most specific → most general. Specific-first.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The introductory search model starts at the specific class.

optionExplanations.A: The introductory search model starts at the specific class.
optionExplanations.B: Starting at the most general class reverses that model.
optionExplanations.C: The described ancestor search is not random class selection.
optionExplanations.D: The three application grouping purposes do not define this lookup sequence.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which inheritance type is AUTOMATIC and uses the shared class-name prefix to determine which ancestors to search?

options.text: Pattern inheritance — automatically searches ancestor classes based on the common naming prefix (e.g., TGB-IT → TGB)
Directed inheritance — explicitly specifies the parent class on the class definition, unrelated to naming patterns
Multiple inheritance — allows a class to inherit from multiple parents simultaneously
Manual inheritance — requires the developer to explicitly copy rules from ancestor classes into the child class

practiceQuiz.hint: Pattern inheritance follows the shared prefix. A Work- parent outside that prefix is an explicit directed relationship.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Shared class-name prefixes identify the pattern mechanism.

optionExplanations.A: Shared class-name prefixes identify the pattern mechanism.
optionExplanations.B: An explicitly specified cross-hierarchy parent is directed inheritance.
optionExplanations.C: The question asks for the documented prefix mechanism, not this alternative label.
optionExplanations.D: Copying does not implement inherited reuse.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An application class must inherit standard Pega platform rules from the Work- class, which is NOT a naming ancestor. Which inheritance type achieves this?

options.text: Directed inheritance — explicitly specified on the class definition to point to a class outside the naming hierarchy
Pattern inheritance — automatically searches ancestors by naming prefix; it automatically finds Work- in the prefix chain
Ruleset inheritance — inheriting from a Ruleset version automatically includes Work- class rules
Delegation — delegating Work- class rules to the child class makes them available in the child's context

practiceQuiz.hint: Cross-hierarchy inheritance = Directed inheritance (explicit parent on class definition).
practiceQuiz.rationale: An explicit parent supports reuse outside the naming hierarchy.

optionExplanations.A: An explicit parent supports reuse outside the naming hierarchy.
optionExplanations.B: Work- is not part of the stated business prefix chain.
optionExplanations.C: Version numbering alone does not establish a class parent.
optionExplanations.D: Business-user delegation is different from class inheritance.

practiceQuiz.scenario: During rule resolution, what is the LAST class Pega searches before returning a 'rule not found' result?

options.text: @baseclass — the ultimate base class that all classes ultimately inherit from; the final stop in rule resolution
The Work-Cover class — the Work-Cover class is the last class checked because it holds the most generic rules
The Integration class — Pega always checks the Integration class last as the system-level fallback
The topmost Ruleset — Pega searches Rulesets in version order and returns 'not found' when the top Ruleset is exhausted

practiceQuiz.hint: Last class in rule resolution chain = @baseclass.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The introductory inheritance search terminates at this ultimate base class.

optionExplanations.A: The introductory inheritance search terminates at this ultimate base class.
optionExplanations.B: Work-Cover is not the ultimate base class named here.
optionExplanations.C: Integration is not a universal final fallback class.
optionExplanations.D: A version container is not the class asked for.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Ticket and Purchase Request Cases should reuse the creator-name property from the shared Work-Cover class described in the source example. Which relationship enables this?

options.text: The configured directed inheritance relationship to the shared ancestor
Delegation to business users — both teams delegate the history rule to their business users who maintain it separately
A shared Ruleset version number — giving both Case Types the same Ruleset version number causes them to share rules
A simultaneous branch merge — merging both branches at the same time causes Pega to deduplicate the history rule

practiceQuiz.hint: The example shares .pxCreateOpName through an explicit ancestor relationship.
practiceQuiz.rationale: The cited property example uses a configured shared ancestor.

optionExplanations.A: The cited property example uses a configured shared ancestor.
optionExplanations.B: Business maintenance does not establish this inherited property relationship.
optionExplanations.C: Equal version numbers alone do not establish inherited behavior.
optionExplanations.D: Merging simultaneously does not establish a shared class ancestor.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A developer needs a variant of an existing routing rule that should apply only to a more-specific class without modifying the original. Which approach should they use?

options.text: Copy (Save As) the Rule into the appropriate child class — the child class's version takes precedence over the ancestor's via rule resolution
Delete the original and rewrite it — removing the original forces all classes to use the new version
Rename the Ruleset — changing the Ruleset name redirects rule resolution to the renamed version for the specific class
Convert it to a Data Page — converting the routing rule to a Data Page makes it class-specific automatically

practiceQuiz.hint: Class-specific override without changing original = Copy (Save As) into the child class.
practiceQuiz.rationale: A suitable child-class copy can specialize the inherited behavior.

optionExplanations.A: A suitable child-class copy can specialize the inherited behavior.
optionExplanations.B: Deleting the shared Rule fails the requirement to preserve it.
optionExplanations.C: Renaming a container does not establish a class-specific Rule variant.
optionExplanations.D: Converting the Rule type does not guarantee equivalent routing or specialization.

practiceQuiz.scenario: To increase a Rule's reusability and avoid creating many near-duplicate versions for small variations, what technique should be applied?

options.text: Parametrization — the rule's logic is driven by a passed-in parameter rather than hard-coded values, enabling one rule to handle many variants
Locking all Rulesets — locking prevents anyone from creating near-duplicate versions, forcing reuse of the existing rule
Adding more patch versions — creating many patch versions of the same rule makes each version serve a different use case
Moving the Rule to the Implementation Layer — implementation-layer rules are automatically reused across all Case Types

practiceQuiz.hint: One rule, many variants via parameters = Parametrization.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Passed parameters allow one Rule to express supported variations.

optionExplanations.A: Passed parameters allow one Rule to express supported variations.
optionExplanations.B: Locking does not by itself express configurable variations.
optionExplanations.C: Many versions are not a replacement for parameterized behavior.
optionExplanations.D: Layer placement alone does not guarantee universal reuse.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A new BA is asking about class hierarchy ownership during project kickoff. Who typically designs the class hierarchy for a new Pega implementation, and when in the project lifecycle is it done?

options.text: The LSA and project leaders typically plan it before building the application
Business users after go-live — business stakeholders refine the class hierarchy based on real usage patterns
The Scrum Master during retrospectives — class hierarchy adjustments are identified and made during sprint retrospectives
The Business Architect in App Studio during Case modeling — class hierarchy is configured automatically as Cases are designed

quickRecap.value: Basic building block defining application behavior. Rules are modular, promoting versioning, delegation, and reuse.
A group of rules packaged for distribution. Versioning follows Major-Minor-Patch (e.g. 01-01-01). Ruleset stack determines the lookup order.
App Studio manages underlying Rules for supported tasks. Dev Studio creates Records with Rule Type, Ruleset, Applies-To class and Label. Generated UI Rule types depend on the architecture/version.
Create menu (Type+app+Ruleset) < App Explorer (+Class) < Rule reference (+Label/ID) < Save As (all, but must change Identifier/Class/Ruleset) | Records explorer: app+Ruleset only.
4 elements: Rule Type internal name + applies-to class + identifier + GMT timestamp. Some types add extra elements (e.g., Correspondence adds type to distinguish email vs. SMS).
Groups rules by reusability: Work, Integration, Data. Hierarchically ordered from most-specific to least-specific.
Automatic reuse based on class name structure. Searches classes sharing a prefix.
Explicitly specified inheritance across different business hierarchies (e.g., inheriting standard Pega classes like Work- or Data-).
